newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine economy expected to sustain growth.
newsitem.headline: Philippine economy expected to sustain growth.

text.p: The Philippines posted 7.1 percent gross national product growth in the first nine months of 1996 and was expected to sustain solid growth in the last quarter, Socioeconomic Planning Secretary Cielito Habito said on Saturday.
GNP, the value of a country's goods and services, grew 5.3 percent in the first nine months of 1995.
This year's growth was fuelled by the recovery of the farm sector, high overseas workers' remittances and the vigorous construction, transport and telecommunications sectors, he said.
Growth in gross domestic product, which represents GNP minus foreign income, was 5.4 percent in the first three quarters versus the year-earlier 4.9 percent.
Habito expected the economy to sustain its robust growth for the rest of the year but said the slowdown in electronics exports was expected to be a setback.
"I believe (1996 GNP) would probably be 7.2 percent," Habito predicted,
The hosting of this month's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit would underpin the economy in the fourth quarter with stronger growth for the services and manufacturing sectors, he said.
Economists said the nine-month GNP figure was mostly in line with expectations and that the government would be able to hit the higher range of its 1996 GNP growth target of 7.0 to 7.5 percent.
A Reuter poll of four economists had earlier showed nine-month GNP expectations at an average 7.16 percent.
"It (1996 GNP) would be a little bit above 7.1 because of the lower exports," said Teedam Navarra, economist at the University of Asia and the Pacific.
"We're still expecting a 7.5 percent GNP growth because of the higher remittances in the fourth quarter," said economist Luz Lorenzo of Peregrine Securities.
Among the components of GNP on the demand side, personal consumption, which accounts for 74 percent of GNP, increased by 4.5 percent in the first nine months from the year-earlier 3.8, Habito said.
Government expenditures, which was 7.9 percent of total GNP, slackened to a 2.6 percent growth from 5.6 due to the streamlining of its operations.
Investments, which take up 24.4 percent of GNP, surged to a double-digit growth of 20.3 from 2.1 percent due to the 16.5 percent expansion in construction, the government said.
Exports of goods and services, comprising 47.7 percent of GNP, rose by 23.1 percent in the last nine months from 14.6 percent.
Exports were primarily driven by overseas income from workers and investments which offset the slowdown in merchandise exports, the government said.

On the supply side, the combined agriculture, fishery and forestry sector rebounded by 3.5 percent in the three quarters compared with a flat 0.8 in the year-ago period on account of better weather conditions.
This segment had a 19.5 percent share of total GNP.
Industry, which took up 34.5 percent of GNP, grew at a slower pace of 6.2 percent from 7.4, dragged down by the 3.19 percent contraction in the mining sector.

And the services sector, which had the biggest share of 41.6 percent, posted a quicker growth of 5.8 percent in the nine months from 5.0, led by the finance, transportation and telecommunications industries. These segments benefitted from the liberalisation programmes of the government, Habito said.
